reconstructed_article: The Victorian Government has approved a $380 million wind farm at Mount Gellibrand in the state's south-west. Planning Minister Rob Hulls announced the decision, describing the project as Australia's most powerful and Victoria's largest wind farm to date. The project is expected to create between 110 and 120 jobs during construction and up to 25 full-time positions during the wind farm's operational life. The wind farm will be located 120 km west of Melbourne, close to the regional centre of Colac. It will comprise 116 turbines of the 2 MW class, with an overall capacity of 232 MW. The facility is expected to produce over 700,000 MWh annually, enough to supply approximately 132,000 Victorian households. German company Pro Ventum International is undertaking the project. Minister Hulls said nine objections had been lodged against the project. Local landowner Tim Gore, who plans to have 32 turbines on his property, said he was not concerned about potential noise. Pro Ventum International said it would commence work on an Environmental Management report in the coming weeks. Wind farm critic Tim Le Roy said there was no environmental benefit from the project and the Victorian Government would better spend its money elsewhere. In October of the previous year, Colac Otway council chief executive officer Tracey Slatter said the proposal would benefit the shire by reducing greenhouse gas emissions and addressing increasing energy demand.

They claim that the government and manufacturers knew of the dangers of asbestos inhalation but failed to take proper precautions, including ceasing to promote asbestos as a cheap construction material and banning its production. After inhaling asbestos in the workplace, 172 people developed lung cancer or mesothelioma, and nearly half of those afflicted have died. Plaintiffs argue that the government and health ministry did not act quickly enough after international organizations issued warnings in 1972 that asbestos could be a carcinogen. They also blame the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry for sanctioning asbestos use under the Factory Act, and the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism for approving asbestos-containing materials under Japan's Building Standards Law. Approximately 40 construction workers plan to file a similar lawsuit in June. Following a 2005 revelation that residents near a factory developed asbestos-related diseases, the government implemented a 2006 law providing monetary assistance to victims and relatives. Plaintiffs argue the assistance is insufficient. Japan had already banned the spraying of asbestos in 1975.

reconstructed_article: On Tuesday at approximately 4:00 a.m., around 500 melon-headed whales were spotted swimming near the shores of Pilar, Bataan, approximately 135 kilometers northwest of Manila. Philippine Coast Guard commander Luis Tuazon and Bataan Governor Enrique Garcia Jr. reported the sighting. More than 100 fishermen and volunteers, along with personnel from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), local police, and the Coast Guard, used dozens of fishing boats with engines shut off to guide the whales toward deeper waters by clapping and hitting the water surface. The mammals were initially wrongly identified as dolphins but were later identified as melon-headed whales by local veterinarian Mariel Flores. Four dead whales were found in Abucay and Tortugas, including two adult females, one pregnant and one that had given birth to a calf that also died. A necropsy by Dr. Lemnuel Aragones of the University of the Philippines found the two adults had damaged eardrums. Provincial veterinarian Alberto Venturina said the adults weighed 250 to 300 kilograms, and the calf was approximately one month old. BFAR director Malcolm Sarmiento Jr. noted this was the largest stranding recorded, with previous events involving only 20 to 30 animals. By 4:30 p.m., rescuers had guided the whales back to deeper waters. Possible causes discussed included underwater earthquakes, chemical pollution, dynamite fishing, and a sea floor earthquake study conducted by the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. PHIVOLCS reported no significant seismic events at the time.

Jost discovered the new species while examining a larger plant collected from the reserve in eastern Ecuador. The reserve was created by a British organization in partnership with Fundacion EcoMinga, for which Jost works. Ecuador has been the site of discovery of more than 1,000 new orchid species in the past century. Jost stated that he found the tiny plant among the roots of another small orchid he had collected and taken to his greenhouse to flower. Months later, he noticed the smaller plant among the roots and recognized it as more significant than the larger orchid. He noted that examining the flower is often the best method for identifying orchid species and determining whether a specimen is unknown. The newly discovered orchid belongs to the same genus as the previous record holder. It is the 60th new orchid species that Dr. Jost has discovered in the past decade.

reconstructed_article: On Friday, the discovery of airborne asbestos in Renaissance Middle School in Montclair, New Jersey, prompted the evacuation of over 200 students and the school's closure. The school, part of Montclair Public Schools, was closed Monday and remained closed Tuesday while undergoing asbestos testing and cleaning. According to a letter sent to parents by the Superintendent's Office of Montclair Public Schools, plaster may have been disturbed during construction on new fire doors on Thursday. An inspection arranged by the school district indicated asbestos was present in the plaster, and a subsequent inspection by asbestos consultant Detail Associates revealed airborne asbestos fiber levels exceeding the acceptable range in the third floor hallway. Business administrator Dana Sullivan stated that testing on March 31 confirmed asbestos in a brown undercoating of plaster. The affected area was sealed off. Public Information Officer Laura Federico said sixth and seventh graders were transported to Hillside Elementary School and eighth graders to another location. Detail Associates conducted cleaning on Saturday. At a Monday meeting between parents and district officials, parents demanded lockers be included in cleanup, prompting Tuesday's closure. Steve Jaraczewski of Detail Associates said one of four test samples was positive for airborne asbestos at over six times acceptable levels. He criticized the asbestos management plan provided by the Archdiocese of Newark, which owns the building. Archdiocese representative Jim Goodness stated the building would reopen soon. The state Department of Environmental Protection is supervising the cleanup.

reconstructed_article: New Jersey school officials acted on Friday after the discovery of airborne asbestos in Renaissance Middle School in Montclair, New Jersey, prompting the evacuation of over 200 students and the school's closure. The school, part of Montclair Public Schools, was closed Monday and remained closed Tuesday while undergoing asbestos testing and cleaning. According to a letter sent to parents by the Superintendent's Office of Montclair Public Schools, plaster may have been disturbed during construction on new fire doors on Thursday. An inspection arranged by the school district indicated asbestos was present in the plaster, and a subsequent inspection by asbestos consultant Detail Associates revealed airborne asbestos fiber levels exceeding the acceptable range in the third floor hallway. Business administrator Dana Sullivan stated that testing on March 31 confirmed asbestos in a brown undercoating of plaster. The affected area was sealed off by district officials. Public Information Officer Laura Federico said sixth and seventh graders were transported to Hillside Elementary School and eighth graders to another location. Detail Associates conducted cleaning on Saturday. At a Monday meeting between parents and district officials, parents demanded lockers be included in cleanup, prompting Tuesday's closure. Steve Jaraczewski of Detail Associates said one of four test samples was positive for airborne asbestos at over six times acceptable levels. He criticized the asbestos management plan provided by the Archdiocese of Newark, which owns the building. Archdiocese representative Jim Goodness stated the building would reopen soon. The state Department of Environmental Protection is supervising the cleanup.

reconstructed_article: The Christchurch Mail Centre in New Zealand was evacuated Friday after employees refused to continue working due to exposure to heavy amounts of dust suspected to be asbestos. Tuam 2 Ltd, the company set to convert the 27-year-old Christchurch Mail Centre into a new city council building, has been aware of the presence of asbestos in the building since May 2008. Hawkins Construction contacted authorities voicing concerns of possible exposure to asbestos material. Testing is currently underway at the facility to determine the nature of the exposure. The Christchurch Mail Centre is operated by New Zealand Post. According to Christchurch Delivery Business Leader Duncan Burman, approximately 50 post workers operate out of the facility, which services about 35,000 addresses in the central Christchurch region. Tony Marryatt, chief executive of the city council, was asked by Councillor Helen Broughton for an explanation of the incident. Broughton, the only councillor who voted against construction of new city council buildings, said she wanted to see the professional opinion from a building consultant who had assessed the building. The owners of the Christchurch Mail Centre informed New Zealand Post that testing performed in November confirmed there was no asbestos in the area. Anna Kenny, a spokesperson for the New Zealand trade union, said concerns were raised about plumes of dust Friday morning suspected to be asbestos, but there has been no confirmation. Kenny confirmed that no asbestos was found in a check of the building in November, but requested further air quality checks before workers return.

He said the result came from voluntary action, with no regulations, levies, or additional costs to shoppers. Major supermarkets are now committed to achieving a 50 per cent reduction goal by the end of this year. Campbell also said development of a viable degradable bag to replace existing lightweight plastic ones is key to further reductions. An estimated 6.67 billion or 36,700 tonnes of plastic bags are disposed of in landfill sites throughout Australia each year. reconstructed_article:
The Australian Government is constructing a $210 million, 800-bed detention facility on Christmas Island, 1400km off Australia's northwest coast. Construction began in January 2005, with the facility scheduled to be operational by late 2006. A DIMIA spokesperson stated the facility would serve as an immigration reception and processing centre, and that a review of mainland detention centres would likely follow its completion.

Christmas Island Shire President Gordon Thompson said residents were concerned about impacts on tourism, restricted access to fishing and snorkelling areas, and lack of consultation. He said the Shire council was not notified when the existing Christmas Island detention centre reopened on November 17 to detain seven West Timorese asylum seekers. Azmi Yon, president of the island's Malay association, said locals sought written clarification on the facility's purpose.

Democrats senator Andrew Bartlett said transferring asylum seekers to the remote location denied them proper processing and legal access. Greens senator Kerry Nettle called for construction to be suspended, citing existing detention capacity of 3,975 people across facilities including Baxter, Villawood, Maribyrnong, Perth, Port Augusta, Port Hedland, and Woomera.

Environmental concerns were raised because the site is adjacent to Abbott's Booby habitat within Christmas Island National Park. Research indicated nesting birds within 300 metres of clearings experienced lower breeding success, with 36% of breeding sites in that zone. The Wilderness Society criticised the government's decision to exempt itself from EPBC Act environmental scrutiny.

reconstructed_article:
The Australian Government is undertaking a $210 million, 800-bed detention facility on Christmas Island, 1400km off Australia's northwest coast. Construction began in January 2005, with the facility scheduled to be operational by late 2006. A DIMIA spokesperson stated the facility would serve as an immigration reception and processing centre, and that a considered review of mainland detention centres would likely follow its completion.

Christmas Island Shire President Gordon Thompson said residents expressed concerns about impacts on tourism, restricted access to fishing and snorkelling areas, and lack of consultation. He said the Shire council was not notified when the existing Christmas Island detention centre reopened on November 17 to detain seven West Timorese asylum seekers. Azmi Yon, president of the island's Malay association, said locals sought written clarification on the facility's purpose.

Democrats senator Andrew Bartlett said transferring asylum seekers to the remote location limited their access to proper processing and legal support. Greens senator Kerry Nettle called for construction to be suspended, citing existing detention capacity of 3,975 people across facilities including Baxter, Villawood, Maribyrnong, Perth, Port Augusta, Port Hedland, and Woomera.

Environmental concerns were raised because the site is adjacent to Abbott's Booby habitat within Christmas Island National Park. Research indicated nesting birds within 300 metres of clearings experienced lower breeding success, with 36% of breeding sites in that zone. The Wilderness Society criticised the government's self-exemption from EPBC Act environmental scrutiny.

reconstructed_article: Following the ousting of Thailand's Prime Minister Yingluck Shinawatra, anti-coup protesters began adopting a three-finger salute—curling the little finger and thumb into the palm and raising the three middle fingers—last weekend in Bangkok. The gesture originates from The Hunger Games book and film series. Thailand's military junta, the National Council for Peace and Order, announced on Tuesday its intent to arrest protesters who display the gesture. Colonel Weerachon Sukhondhapatipak told the Associated Press that authorities are monitoring the movement and will control obvious forms of resistance to prevent disorder. Colonel Winthai Suwaree expressed a similar sentiment to media. The coup, reportedly Thailand's fourteenth since the adoption of constitutional monarchy in 1932, followed political deadlock from demonstrations spanning seven months. A midnight-to-4 a.m. curfew remains in effect, with Phuket and other beach resorts exempted to protect the tourist industry. The United States Department of State advised citizens to reconsider non-essential travel to Thailand and avoid protest groups. The junta imposed internet censorship, television broadcast restrictions, and banned political assemblies of five or more people. On Sunday, approximately 6,000 soldiers and police officers were deployed in Bangkok. Protesters also used flash mobs and masked walks through the central shopping district. Some protesters interpreted the gesture as representing freedom, election, and democracy. Social activist Sombat Boonngam-anong, belonging to a protest group supporting the Shinawatra governments, advocated silent protest raising three fingers three times daily for 30 seconds at 9 a.m., 1 p.m., and 5 p.m.

reconstructed_article: The People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD), a Thai anti-government movement, carried out a campaign of disruption designated the 'King Taksin operation,' named after an 18th-century Siamese monarch. PAD protesters began massing on Sunday and blockaded the parliament building on Monday morning, forcing the cancellation of joint MP and Senate sessions. The PAD stated it would persist in disrupting parliamentary sessions until parliament went into recess or the government resigned. The PAD opposes proposed constitutional changes. The government stated these changes were not on Monday's agenda and that ASEAN-related legislation was to be discussed instead. Thailand, the current chair of ASEAN, faced concerns about its ability to ratify treaties at an upcoming meeting in northern Thailand. With parliament inactive, PAD protesters targeted additional government offices, including the temporary cabinet location at the old Bangkok international airport. The government had operated from mothballed buildings there since the PAD commandeered the main Government House compound in late August. A PAD call for a public sector strike met with limited response. The government of Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat of the People Power Party (PPP) was the target. Authorities avoided confrontation following clashes the previous month in which two protesters were killed when police used tear gas. Police allowed protesters to lay siege to the empty parliament building. Deposed former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, in self-imposed exile and facing a two-year prison sentence in Thailand, stated in an interview with Abu Dhabi's Arabian Business his intention to return to politics. He condemned the UK government for revoking his visa. He was believed to be staying in Dubai.

reconstructed_article: Corus, the world's fifth largest steel producer, announced on Friday that it may mothball its steelworks in Teesside, England, threatening the jobs of 1,920 employees. Corus may close its Teesside operations after a consortium refused to honour a 10-year contract with Corus' Teesside Cast Products, which accounted for 78% of the plant's operations. Corus' chief executive, Kirby Adams, said he was extremely disappointed that the consortium members had taken this action. Business Secretary Peter Mandelson said it is essential that Corus does everything it can legally, and with the government's assistance, to reinstate the agreement. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown said the government was doing everything in its power to ensure that the contract is upheld. Mandelson also said the government was not prepared to reconcile itself to the inevitable closure of the plant. The leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, Councillor George Dunning, described the announcement as being hit by a mini earthquake. Liberal Democrats including Simon Hughes, Fiona Hall, and Stephen Hughes MEP supported the idea that the government should subsidise wages at the plant on a temporary basis. Hughes and Hall suggested the government should apply to the EU's European Globalisation Fund. Adams said the move could bring to an end a proud heritage of steelmaking at Teesside. Corus said a 90-day consultation period is due to begin. Corus' owner, Tata Steel, is also facing difficulties with another UK operation, automobile company Jaguar Land Rover.

reconstructed_article: Australian transport investigators identified a safety issue with engines fitted to Airbus A380 passenger airliners. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said some Rolls-Royce Trent 900 engines may be prone to fatigue cracking, which could lead to oil leakage and fire. The ATSB said this was central to the engine failure on a Qantas A380 on November 4, shortly after take-off from Singapore. Qantas grounded all six of its A380 fleet for safety checks before returning them to service. The ATSB said the manufacturing fault could lead to an elevated risk of fatigue crack initiation and growth, oil leakage, and a resulting oil fire. The agency, which is responsible for such investigations, urged Rolls-Royce to address the safety issue and take actions necessary to ensure the safety of flight operations in aircraft equipped with Trent 900 series engines. Qantas stated there was no immediate risk to flight safety but would conduct further investigations. Two A380 aircraft were in operational service, with both to be inspected at the Qantas Jet Base in Sydney. Two other airlines, Lufthansa and Singapore Airlines, use A380 aircraft with Trent engines. Singapore Airlines said it was checking its A380 engines on a daily basis and would carry out the new ATSB-advised checks as quickly as possible. The A380 made its first commercial flight in 2007 and has a maximum capacity of 840 passengers, though Qantas' can carry 450.

reconstructed_article: L. Alan Winters, professor of economics at the University of Sussex and founding director of the UK Trade Policy Observatory (UKTPO), was interviewed about UK trade policy following Brexit. Winters stated he was opposed to Brexit and considers it poor economic policy, arguing the UK would have been better off with a tighter relationship with Europe to keep trade costs lower. He co-authored reports including "The Costs of Brexit," "COVID-19 will reinforce the Brexit shock," and "Taking stock of the new UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement." Winters said Brexit and COVID-19 shocks interact, making recovery from lost export markets harder. He dismissed the idea that trade with distant partners like Australia, New Zealand, or CPTPP members could replace EU trade, noting the EU represents approximately half of UK trade and that benefits of trade agreements weaken with distance. On fishing, he noted the UK gained some quota transfer but must still prove compliance with EU standards to sell fish in Europe. He criticized government statistics presenting 218 billion in rolled-over trade as new income. Regarding the Northern Ireland Protocol, he attributed complications to Brexit and the specific form of Brexit chosen by Boris Johnson. Winters argued the UK should pursue a quiet, cooperative role in the WTO and urged the G7 to focus on repairing the multilateral trading system rather than pursuing bilateral photo opportunities. He expressed concern about rising Chinese-Western tensions and cautioned against framing democratic cooperation in an anti-China light. He called for greater domestic debate on trade policy, noting the executive faces few constraints.

Alan Winters, professor of economics at the University of Sussex and founding director of the UK Trade Policy Observatory (UKTPO), was interviewed about UK trade policy following Brexit. Winters, a vocal opponent of Brexit, considers it poor economic policy, arguing the UK would have been better off with a tighter relationship with Europe to keep trade costs lower. He co-authored reports including "The Costs of Brexit," "COVID-19 will reinforce the Brexit shock," and "Taking stock of the new UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement." Winters said Brexit and COVID-19 shocks interact, making recovery from lost export markets harder. He dismissed the idea that trade with distant partners like Australia, New Zealand, or CPTPP members could replace EU trade, noting the EU represents approximately half of UK trade and that benefits of trade agreements weaken with distance. On fishing, he noted the UK gained some quota transfer but must still prove compliance with EU standards to sell fish in Europe. He took issue with government statistics presenting £218 billion in rolled-over trade as new income. Regarding the Northern Ireland Protocol, he attributed complications to Brexit and the specific form of Brexit chosen by Boris Johnson. Winters argued the UK should pursue a quiet, cooperative role in the WTO and urged the G7 to focus on repairing the multilateral trading system rather than pursuing bilateral photo opportunities. He expressed concern about rising Chinese-Western tensions and cautioned against framing democratic cooperation in an anti-China light. He called for greater domestic debate on trade policy, noting the executive faces few constraints.

reconstructed_article: U.S. officials announced new plans requiring air traffic controllers to have longer rest periods between shifts after a series of incidents in which controllers fell asleep on duty at airports across the country. Transport Secretary LaHood said he was outraged by the incidents. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the U.S. government agency responsible for aviation, said the plans would be implemented promptly. The announcement came after another controller was suspended this week for falling asleep while directing aircraft near [location]. This was the sixth such incident this year, with controllers having fallen asleep in Nevada, Washington D.C., and Tennessee. In one incident, two commercial passenger jets landed without direction from the control tower because the controller had fallen asleep. Under the new plans, controllers must have a minimum of nine hours rest between shifts, an increase of one hour. More supervisors will be required during night shifts, and controllers will be restricted in what shifts they can swap with colleagues. LaHood said controllers who fall asleep on duty will face consequences. Earlier this week, the head of the air traffic organization at the FAA resigned after LaHood called the crisis unacceptable. The results of a study on how fatigue affects controllers will soon be published, and the FAA may make further changes. The union representing controllers in the U.S. said it had full support for the new, constructive steps.

reconstructed_article: Roger D. Kornberg of the United States won the 2006 Nobel Prize for chemistry for his studies of the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription. Kornberg's work explains how information encoded in DNA is used to produce the proteins that keep cells functioning. Eukaryotes are multi-celled organisms, such as animals, plants and fungi, which have their genetic material stored in nuclei within their cells. To use their genetic information, eukaryotes extract bits of the coded information via the formation of messenger RNA, which consists of copies of a particular gene within the DNA strand. Translation takes place when proteins are built from the information transcribed with the messenger RNA. Eukaryotic transcription is vital for life. If transcription is interrupted, as can happen when cells are exposed to certain toxins, the cells will die. Kornberg documented eukaryotic transcription with snapshots of the process in action. He created the snapshots by crystallizing cellular material partway through transcription and exposing them to x-rays that produced patterns revealing the intermediate structures. Kornberg's work may lead to novel drugs and medical treatments. Kornberg's father Arthur Kornberg won the Nobel Prize in physiology and medicine in 1959 for explaining how organisms synthesize DNA from nucleotides.

An organizer at the Wikimedia Foundation offices in St. Petersburg, Florida, said that planning discussions began before the Wikimania location was announced and that the conference was not created in retaliation or to compete with Wikimania. He said the goal is to provide a Wikimedia event for the western hemisphere, noting that travel to Egypt is more expensive for people in the region. Over 100 interested parties across the United States have expressed interest in volunteering or attending. The conference will cover Wikimedia and the free culture movement in relation to communities in North America, including the United States and Canada, and Latin America. A journalism segment will be held at the Turner Broadcasting building on Techwood Drive in Midtown Atlanta. Wikimedia Argentina and the Wikimedia Foundation have received proposals for endorsement, with decisions pending. Sponsors include Georgia Tech, the Public Journalism Network, and the Carolina Open Source Initiative. The selection of Alexandria for Wikimania 2008 prompted discussion on public mailing lists regarding safety, free speech, and the jury's decision process.

reconstructed_article: The Christchurch Mail Centre in New Zealand was evacuated Friday after employees declined to continue working due to exposure to heavy amounts of dust suspected to be asbestos. Tuam 2 Ltd, the company set to convert the 27-year-old Christchurch Mail Centre into a new city council building, has been aware of the presence of asbestos in the building since May 2008. Hawkins Construction contacted authorities voicing concerns of possible exposure to asbestos material. Testing is currently underway at the facility to determine the nature of the exposure. The Christchurch Mail Centre is operated by New Zealand Post. According to Christchurch Delivery Business Leader Duncan Burman, approximately 50 post workers operate out of the facility, which services about 35,000 addresses in the central Christchurch region. Tony Marryatt, chief executive of the city council, was asked by Councillor Helen Broughton for an explanation of the incident. Broughton, the only councillor who voted against construction of new city council buildings, said she wanted to see the professional opinion from a building consultant who had assessed the building. The owners of the Christchurch Mail Centre informed New Zealand Post that testing performed in November confirmed there was no asbestos in the area. Anna Kenny, a spokesperson for the New Zealand trade union, said concerns were raised about plumes of dust Friday morning suspected to be asbestos, but there has been no confirmation. Kenny confirmed that no asbestos was found in a check of the building in November, but requested further air quality checks before workers return.

reconstructed_article: American botanist Lou Jost has discovered the world's smallest orchid among the roots of a larger plant in a nature reserve in Ecuador. The flowers measure 2.1mm wide and have transparent petals that are one cell thick. The finding surpasses the previous record held by Platystele jungermannioides, which has 2.5mm flowers. Jost discovered the new species accidentally while examining a larger plant collected from the reserve in eastern Ecuador. The reserve was created by a British organization in partnership with Fundacion EcoMinga, for which Jost works. Ecuador has been the site of discovery of more than 1,000 new orchid species in the past century. Jost stated that he found the tiny plant among the roots of another small orchid he had collected and taken to his greenhouse to flower. Months later, he noticed the smaller plant among the roots and recognized it as more significant than the larger orchid. He noted that examining the flower is often the best method for identifying orchid species and determining whether a specimen is unknown. The newly discovered orchid belongs to the same genus as the previous record holder. It is the 60th new orchid species that Dr. Jost has discovered in the past decade.

On Friday, 178 plaintiffs, including construction workers and family members of deceased workers, filed a lawsuit in Tokyo, Japan, seeking approximately 6.6 billion yen (about 64 million USD) in damages from the Japanese government and 46 building manufacturers. According to reports, the class action is the first in Japan related to health damages caused by asbestos exposure at construction sites. The plaintiffs are from Tokyo and surrounding areas.

reconstructed_article: Corus, the world's fifth largest steel producer, announced on Friday that it may be forced to mothball its steelworks in Teesside, England, threatening the jobs of 1,920 employees. Corus may be forced to close its Teesside operations as a consortium has refused to honour a 10-year contract with Corus' Teesside Cast Products, which accounted for 78% of the plant's operations. Corus' chief executive, Kirby Adams, said he was disappointed that the consortium members had taken this action. Business Secretary Peter Mandelson said it is essential that Corus does everything it can legally, and with the government's assistance, to reinstate the agreement. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown said the government was doing everything in its power to ensure that the contract is upheld. Mandelson also said the government was not prepared to reconcile itself to the inevitable closure of the plant. The leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, Councillor George Dunning, described the announcement as being hit by a mini earthquake. Liberal Democrats including Simon Hughes, Fiona Hall, and Stephen Hughes MEP supported the idea that the government should subsidise wages at the plant on a temporary basis. Hughes and Hall suggested the government should apply to the EU's European Globalisation Fund. Adams said the move could bring to an end a heritage of steelmaking at Teesside. Corus said a 90-day consultation period is due to begin. Corus' owner, Tata Steel, is also facing difficulties with another UK operation, automobile company Jaguar Land Rover.

The ATSB said the manufacturing fault could lead to an elevated risk of fatigue crack initiation and growth, oil leakage, and a resulting oil fire. The agency urged Rolls-Royce to address the safety issue and take actions necessary to ensure the safety of flight operations in aircraft equipped with Trent 900 series engines. Singapore Airlines said it was checking its A380 engines on a daily basis and would carry out the new ATSB-advised checks as quickly as possible. The A380 made its first commercial flight in 2007 and has a maximum capacity of 840 passengers, though Qantas' can carry 450.

reconstructed_article: NASA disclosed that a three-inch gouge was found in the heat shield on one of Endeavour's wings. The gouge was observed as the shuttle approached the International Space Station (ISS) and was captured on camera by ISS astronauts. According to NASA, the gouge was located on a six-inch thick tile on the starboard wing of the heat shield and may have been caused by ice rather than foam. NASA expressed concern because the hole appears to be deep. Mission management team chairman John Shannon stated that the assessment would involve thermal analysis based on the damage, a review of flight history, and testing of the area. He noted that it was too early to determine whether repairs were required. If the damage is irreversible and cannot be fixed, the Endeavour crew would remain on the ISS. NASA stated that supplies would last until a rescue mission could be launched on October 8. During Endeavour's liftoff on August 8, cameras showed moisture on the lens, but the object causing the damage was not captured. At least nine pieces of debris were filmed during takeoff, though NASA said only three had a possibility of hitting the shuttle. Astronauts were expected to use a laser attached to the shuttle's robotic arm to measure the gouge's depth and size on Sunday. Potential repairs included affixing a metal plate over the tile, filling it with putty, or sealing the gouge.

BAD stated that in the United Kingdom alone, nearly 30% of the population suffers from rashes caused by prolonged exposure to nickel. Researchers recommended that individuals purchase swab test kits to test for traces of nickel.

reconstructed_article: The 108-floor central component of the new World Trade Center in New York City has been officially renamed 1 World Trade Center, ending the Freedom Tower name it had carried since 2003. The building is on track for completion in 2013, with 10 floors partially finished. Port Authority of New York and New Jersey Chairman Anthony Coscia said the name is easiest for people to identify with and has received a warm reception. Former Governor George Pataki, who revealed the Freedom Tower name nearly six years ago, criticized the switch, stating the building is not simply real estate or a marketing name. 1 World Trade Center has been the building's legal name and address for two years, with the public change driven by increased construction and lease marketing. Mayor Michael Bloomberg expressed ambivalence, saying he preferred the Freedom Tower name but acknowledged that if renaming helps rent the building, it is the responsible action. The change followed the signing of a two-decade lease by a Chinese real estate company planning to occupy floors 64 through 69. Other future tenants include the federal government and the New York State Office of General Services.

reconstructed_article: The World Bank released its 2012 World Development Report on Gender Equality and Development. The report mentions India over 300 times, compared with Spain at 48, Canada at 22, and New Zealand at 15. The report states that gender equality contributes to productivity, outcomes for the next generation, and representative decision making. In India, improved local-level gender equality correlated with meaningful improvements in sanitation, water supplies, irrigation, and schools. Nationally, a woman's income correlated positively with years her children spent in school. No gender gap exists in attendance for the richest 20% of Indian families, but males outnumber females 5 to 1 among the poorest 20%. Girls in the bottom 20% average completion of Grade 1; males average Grade 6. By age 15, parents in Andhra Pradesh prioritize outcomes for male children over female ones. Indian women earn $0.64 for every $1 earned by men, compared with $0.62 in Germany, $0.60 in Georgia, $0.90 in Malawi, $0.82 in Egypt, and $0.80 in Benin and Mexico. A fifth of married Indian women do not control household spending decisions, an 18% average matching Mozambique, between Nigeria at 14% and Zambia and Rwanda at 20%. India reduced average children per woman from six to three in 35 years, compared with 100 years in the United States. India's maternal mortality rate is six times that of Sri Lanka. Excess female deaths in India dropped by 8,000, from 265,000 in 1990 to 257,000 in 2008; in China they grew by 202,000.

reconstructed_article: International twin-study researchers conducted parallel genetic studies into bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, examining more than 50,000 people worldwide. Eleven genetic regions were identified; seven were for schizophrenia, five of which were previously undiscovered. Two genetic loci were associated with both diseases. The studies scanned genomes of both healthy and afflicted individuals. Researchers found that genetic factors are numerous rather than a single faulty gene. In schizophrenia, at most around 30% of genetic components are thought to have been identified. Pablo Gejman, a lead researcher on the schizophrenia study, stated that one goal of genetic research is to find druggable targets. He identified calcium-activated channels in the brain as promising candidates for new drugs, linked to schizophrenia in the study. A genetic locus called mir137 suggests an abnormality of gene regulation. The team found no evidence that dopamine receptors are involved, though current drug treatments target them. Professor Rodney Scott from the University of Newcastle in Australia noted the strength of the research lies in its numbers, providing robust statistical power. Both Gejman and Scott described the study as highly reliable due to its sample size. Scott noted that the two shared genetic loci are suggestive of a potential common pathway giving rise to both diseases. Gejman called it an excellent demonstration because the same chains are common to both disorders. Each illness affects approximately 1% of people. The diseases are poorly understood, and it remains uncertain whether they are components of a single spectrum or comprise multiple illnesses.

reconstructed_article: On Tuesday, the World Bank released the 2012 World Development Report on Gender Equality and Development. The report uses the United States as a benchmark for understanding gains for women globally while noting that US women still lag behind US men in several areas. The authors find that US women are disproportionately represented in teaching and nursing, paid less than male counterparts, and under-represented at the highest business levels, with only 28 of Fortune 1000 companies having a female CEO. Women in the bottom 20% economically have a slightly higher birth rate than those in the top 20%. Immigrants from Southeast Asia and India show higher than expected male-to-female birth ratios, which authors attribute partly to deliberate sex selection based on cultural attitudes. In 2009, over half a million US women were victims of intimate partner violence. US men hold greater pension assets, and elderly women are more likely to live alone than with a spouse. Women account for less than 20% of local police officers and bear 61% of housework duties. High childcare costs disincentivize women from re-entering the workforce after giving birth. The report notes that major gains took considerable time: it took 40 years (1870-1910) to see major improvements in girls' school attendance aged 6-12. In 1921, after women obtained suffrage, Congress passed legislation that helped lower infant mortality from 23% to 15%. Property rights for women began by 1848 in New York. The report cites research showing that higher maternal education improves children's outcomes.

Women account for less than 20% of local police officers and bear 61% of housework duties. High childcare costs disincentivize women from re-entering the workforce after giving birth.

In 1921, after women obtained suffrage, Congress passed legislation that helped lower infant mortality from 23% to 15%. Property rights for women began by 1848 in New York. The report cites research showing that higher maternal education improves children's outcomes.

The city is now surrounded by barriers and checkpoints and is being searched by troops, but no fighting has been reported. The Interior Minister reported 1,068 arrests, adding that 94 have been cleared and released. Several of those arrested were in high and mid-level positions in the command structure of al-Qaeda, including suicide bomb cell leaders and people who arranged for foreign fighters to enter Iraq. The Prime Minister has promised an amnesty to fighters who surrender their weapons provided they have not killed civilians.

Maribel, who knows very little English, claimed that the boy initiated the conflict; the boy admitted as much.

Ono stated that "it is a pity that this decision weakens the rights of all copyright owners" and plans to appeal.

reconstructed_article: Matthew Wright, host of British television programme The Wright Stuff, apologised for remarks made on the show regarding the murder of Liam Aitchison. During the edition broadcast on Tuesday, Wright said "there's been another murder" in a false Scottish accent, referencing the UK television crime drama Taggart. Panelist Charlie Baker remarked the investigation would be like "the longest episode of Taggart of all time," and the audience laughed. Liam Aitchison's family issued a statement calling the comments "insensitive and offensive" and "very upsetting and insulting for, not just the family, but for the whole community of the Western Isles." His father, Norman Aitchison, wrote on the programme's website that he was "disgusted" and asked whether panel members would joke if it were their own child. On the following day's broadcast, Wright said he would "like to apologise" if viewers were offended, stating there was no intention to belittle the tragedy. Channel 5's spokeswoman said Wright's apology was "clear." Wright noted he had not been helped by campaigns urging people to report him to Ofcom, a UK media regulator, and advised such people to "grow up." Channel 5 removed Tuesday's episode from its website. Angus MacNeil, MP for Na h-Eileanan an Iar, described Wright's behaviour as "beyond belief" and intended to complain to Ofcom. Comhairle nan Eilean Siar also complained. A Facebook page titled "Report The Wright Stuff to Ofcom" attracted over two thousand likes. Ofcom was assessing complaints but had not decided whether to investigate.

reconstructed_article: Matthew Wright, host of British television programme The Wright Stuff, apologised for remarks he made on the show regarding the murder of Liam Aitchison. During the edition broadcast on Tuesday, Wright said "there's been another murder" in a false Scottish accent, referencing the UK television crime drama Taggart. Panelist Charlie Baker remarked the investigation would be like "the longest episode of Taggart of all time," and the audience laughed. Liam Aitchison's family issued a statement calling the comments "insensitive and offensive" and "very upsetting and insulting for, not just the family, but for the whole community of the Western Isles." His father, Norman Aitchison, wrote on the programme's website that he was "disgusted" and asked whether panel members would joke if it were their own child. On the following day's broadcast, Wright said he would "like to apologise" if viewers were offended, stating he had no intention to belittle the tragedy. Wright noted he had not been helped by campaigns urging people to report him to Ofcom, a UK media regulator, and advised such people to "grow up." Channel 5's spokeswoman said Wright's apology was "clear." Channel 5 removed Tuesday's episode from its website. Angus MacNeil, MP for Na h-Eileanan an Iar, described Wright's behaviour as "beyond belief" and intended to complain to Ofcom. Comhairle nan Eilean Siar also complained. A Facebook page titled "Report The Wright Stuff to Ofcom" attracted over two thousand likes. Ofcom was assessing complaints but had not decided whether to investigate.

reconstructed_article: On Thursday, the U.S. House of Representatives voted 269-152 to reject the Net Neutrality Amendment to the COPE Act. The House then passed the COPE Act, which would make it easier for telecommunications companies to offer cable TV service and affect competition in that sector, by a 321-101 vote the same day. Proponents said it would lower high-speed Internet prices by enabling providers to bundle phone, data, video, and mobile services. Opponents said it would not lower prices or said the price effects were uncertain. It was the first major telecommunications bill before Congress in over a decade. The Net Neutrality amendment sought to require broadband providers to treat all data equally, specifying a duty not to block, impair, degrade, discriminate against, or interfere with access to lawful content, applications, or services. Its passage would have prevented companies such as AT&T, Verizon, and Comcast from charging content providers like Google, Yahoo, Amazon, or eBay for priority network access. Democrats largely supported the amendment, with 140 voting in favor and 58 against, while 11 Republicans voted for it and 211 against. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi argued that additional fees would burden small web-based businesses and hamper noncommercial communications. Phone companies and Congressional allies argued the restrictions would discourage investment in network upgrades. The bill is due to be discussed next in the Senate.

Phone companies and their Congressional allies argued the restrictions would discourage investment in network upgrades.

The bill is due to be discussed next in the Senate.

Police in Purcell, Oklahoma, approximately 40 miles (64 km) south of Oklahoma City, discovered the body of ten-year-old Jamie Rose Bolin on Friday in the apartment of Kevin Underwood, 26, a resident of the same apartment complex. Underwood was arrested on suspicion of first-degree murder and held without bail. He had no prior criminal record or history of mental illness.

Bolin was last seen on Wednesday near the Purcell public library, and her family reported her missing that night. Officials issued an Amber Alert on Thursday night, noting that no abduction had been reported initially.

Underwood drew suspicion at an information checkpoint set up at the apartment complex. Tim Kuykendall, district attorney for McClain County, said the body was found in a storage bin in the bedroom closet. Police found a decorative dagger, hacksaw, barbecue skewers, meat tenderizer, and wooden cutting board in his apartment.

Preliminary autopsy reports indicated Bolin died of asphyxiation and blunt force trauma to the head. Authorities said deep saw marks on the body indicated an attempt to decapitate her. Police suspected postmortem molestation, as the body was found unclothed.

Purcell police chief David Tompkins stated the motive appeared to involve a plan to kidnap, rape, torture, kill, decapitate, drain of blood, rape the corpse, eat the corpse, and dispose of the organs and bones. Kuykendall said Underwood reported fantasizing about eating someone beginning a year prior. Authorities believed other individuals, including a woman and a 5-year-old boy, had been targeted and considered. Kuykendall stated he intended to seek the death penalty.

reconstructed_article: On Tuesday at approximately 4:00 a.m., around 500 melon-headed whales were spotted swimming near the shores of Pilar, Bataan, approximately 135 kilometers northwest of Manila. Philippine Coast Guard commander Luis Tuazon and Bataan Governor Enrique Garcia Jr. mobilized in response to the sighting, coordinating an effort to protect the animals. More than 100 fishermen and volunteers, along with personnel from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), local police, and the Coast Guard, were deployed and used dozens of fishing boats with engines shut off to guide the whales toward deeper waters by clapping and hitting the water surface. The mammals were initially misidentified as dolphins but were later identified as melon-headed whales by local veterinarian Mariel Flores. Four dead whales were found in Abucay and Tortugas, including two adult females, one pregnant and one that had given birth to a calf that also died. A necropsy by Dr. Lemnuel Aragones of the University of the Philippines found the two adults had damaged eardrums. Provincial veterinarian Alberto Venturina said the adults weighed 250 to 300 kilograms, and the calf was approximately one month old. BFAR director Malcolm Sarmiento Jr. noted this was the largest stranding recorded, with previous events involving only 20 to 30 animals. By 4:30 p.m., authorities and volunteers had guided the whales back to deeper waters. Possible causes discussed included underwater earthquakes, chemical pollution, dynamite fishing, and a sea floor earthquake study conducted by the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. PHIVOLCS reported no significant seismic events at the time.

reconstructed_article: U.S. District Judge Stein ruled that the use of a 25-second clip from John Lennon's song "Imagine" in a film critical of religion is likely defensible under the fair use doctrine. The film "Expelled," produced by Premise Media and starring comedian Ben Stein, deploys the clip to represent what Premise representative Anthony Falzone described at a hearing as "the most popular and persuasive embodiment of this viewpoint that the world is better off without religion." In the song, Lennon proposes the hypothetical "Imagine there's no heaven ... and no religion too." On April 23, 2008, Lennon's widow, Yoko Ono, along with his sons Sean and Julian, and music producer EMI Blackwood, Inc., filed suit against Premise Media for alleged copyright infringement, as the song had not been licensed for use in the film. On May 19, a preliminary injunction was issued preventing distribution of the film. On June 2, Judge Stein ruled that the fair use defense would likely succeed and lifted the injunction, writing that "the fair use of a copyrighted work for the purposes of criticism and commentary is not an infringement of copyright." "Expelled" is a documentary claiming that intelligent design proponents are being suppressed by the scientific community. It has received criticism from scientists and film critics and has faced additional copyright claims over animated sequences resembling "The Inner Life of the Cell," produced by XVIVO and Harvard University. Ono stated that "it is a pity that this decision weakens the rights of all copyright owners" and plans to appeal.

reconstructed_article:
The World Bank released its 2012 World Development Report on Gender Equality and Development. The report mentions India over 300 times, compared with Spain at 48, Canada at 22, and New Zealand at 15. The World Bank states in the report that gender equality contributes to productivity, outcomes for the next generation, and representative decision making.

In India, improved local-level gender equality correlated with improvements in sanitation, water supplies, irrigation, and schools. Nationally, a woman's income correlated positively with years her children spent in school. No gender gap exists in attendance for the richest 20% of Indian families, but males outnumber females 5 to 1 among the poorest 20%. Girls in the bottom 20% average completion of Grade 1; males average Grade 6. By age 15, parents in Andhra Pradesh prioritize outcomes for male children over female ones.

Indian women earn $0.64 for every $1 earned by men, compared with $0.62 in Germany, $0.60 in Georgia, $0.90 in Malawi, $0.82 in Egypt, and $0.80 in Benin and Mexico. A fifth of married Indian women do not control household spending decisions, an 18% average matching Mozambique, between Nigeria at 14% and Zambia and Rwanda at 20%.

India reduced average children per woman from six to three in 35 years, compared with 100 years in the United States. India's maternal mortality rate is six times that of Sri Lanka. Excess female deaths in India dropped by 8,000, from 265,000 in 1990 to 257,000 in 2008; in China they grew by 202,000.

Ministers from thirteen Asian countries pledged on Friday to double the wild tiger population on the continent to seven thousand by 2022. The commitment came at Asia's first ministerial conference on tiger conservation in Thailand.

The thirteen countries that endorsed the pledge were Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, China, India, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Russia, Thailand, and Vietnam, all countries where the wild Asian tiger is still found.

Thai Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva stated in a video address that the wild tiger is in crisis and that this may be the last chance to save it.

The meeting was partially organized by the Global Tiger Initiative, a coalition within the World Bank, as well as the Smithsonian Institution and various conservation groups.

Meeting host Suwit Khunkitti, Thailand's minister of natural resources and environment, noted that there were 100,000 tigers across range countries 100 years ago, compared to about 3,500 today.

According to the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), tiger numbers have declined due to poaching. The animals live in only seven percent of the territory they occupied a hundred years ago, according to Voice of America.

WWF representative Michael Baltzer said it was important to act during the Year of the Tiger.

Global Tiger Initiative program director Keshav Varma said saving the tiger also preserves habitat for other species and draws attention to issues including encroachment and corruption.

reconstructed_article:
Corus, the world's fifth largest steel producer, announced on Friday that its steelworks in Teesside, England, may be mothballed, threatening the jobs of 1,920 employees. The possible closure follows a consortium's refusal to honour a 10-year contract with Corus' Teesside Cast Products, which accounted for 78% of the plant's operations.

Corus' chief executive, Kirby Adams, said he was extremely disappointed that the consortium members had taken this action. Business Secretary Peter Mandelson said it is essential that Corus does everything it can legally, and with the government's assistance, to reinstate the agreement. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown said the government was doing everything in its power to ensure that the contract is upheld. Mandelson also said the government was not prepared to reconcile itself to the inevitable closure of the plant.

The leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, Councillor George Dunning, described the announcement as being hit by a mini earthquake. Liberal Democrats including Simon Hughes, Fiona Hall, and Stephen Hughes MEP supported the idea that the government should subsidise wages at the plant on a temporary basis. Hughes and Hall suggested the government should apply to the EU's European Globalisation Fund.

Adams said the move could bring to an end a heritage of steelmaking at Teesside. A 90-day consultation period is due to begin, Corus said. Corus' owner, Tata Steel, is also facing difficulties with another UK operation, automobile company Jaguar Land Rover.
